title: Giving Feedback to Team Members Who Overcorrect
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece explains why team members sometimes overcorrect after receiving feedback -- applying a compliment or criticism far more broadly, intensely, or rigidly than the leader intended. Through several worked examples (an assistant who over-edits every email, a colleague who becomes excessively quiet after being told they interrupt too much), the author shows how vague feedback scales behavior unpredictably while precise feedback calibrates it. The recommended fix is specifying the scope, intensity, duration, and conditions attached to any praise or correction, rather than withholding feedback out of fear of being misread.
points: Overcorrection happens when a team member applies praise or criticism too broadly, too intensely, or too rigidly.
Worked examples show how a compliment on conciseness produced one-sentence replies, and praise for responsiveness produced round-the-clock messaging.
The fix isn't withholding feedback but specifying exactly when, where, and how much the feedback should apply.
Vague feedback tends to scale behavior unpredictably; precise, conditional feedback calibrates it instead.
quotes: Overcorrection occurs when a colleague receives praise or criticism and then responds by applying it too broadly, too intensely, or too rigidly.
A manager who compliments a team member for being responsive later finds the colleague responding to messages at all hours, even on weekends.
The solution is not to withhold feedback but to make clear when and where it applies. When leaders fear overcorrection, they must specify the conditions that go with the message.
Overcorrection can be avoided when leaders define the scope, intensity, duration, and conditions under which the feedback applies.
Leaders need to remember that team members don’t just hear feedback. They infer expectations for the future. Vague feedback can sometimes scale behavior. More precise feedback calibrates it.
